classification.rationale: The source is a podcast transcript featuring a discussion on consciousness, computation, and AI, with no direct UFO/UAP content. It is classified as media content, with primary hints for topic and key figure extraction.

provenance.source: YouTube interview with Professor William Hahn at MIT Media Lab

primary_claims: Consciousness is not binary but a hierarchy of representations of representations, attributed to Leibniz.
Modern AI systems are intelligent but may not be conscious; they might lack self-representation.
It is almost inevitable that AI will eventually achieve consciousness if current trends continue.
Wolfram's principle of computational equivalence suggests that universal computation is common in nature.
Natural systems, including rocks and GPUs, can be considered computational objects.
There may be unthinkable thoughts beyond human conceptual and perceptual windows.
The mind may have an 'immune system' that filters out destabilizing thoughts.
Language may not be sufficient to express all thoughts; some ideas are non-decomposable.
Language can be viewed as a 'divine parasite' living on the brain, evidenced by multiple personality phenomena.
The brain may be a programmable object, and natural language may be a programming language.
key_findings: Interview conducted at MIT Media Lab with Professor William Hahn.
Discussion references Stephen Wolfram's computational equivalence and Leibniz's hierarchy of representations.
Mentions of 'early 2025' as the time of the conversation.
References to previous podcast appearances and Jacob Barndes podcast.
Mentions of colleague Dr. Behrenholz regarding language as an organism.
Mentions of Richard Hamming's ideas on perceptual limits.
Mentions of Graham's number as an example of inconceivable numbers.
Mentions of 'umwelt' as a philosophical term.
Mentions of 'Turing tar pit' and computer languages like BASIC and C.
Mentions of 'conlangs' and 'esoteric languages' as potential sources of new thought.
supporting_evidence: Wolfram's cellular automata research showing universal computation arises from simple rules.
Examples of emulators running on emulators as a model for layered virtual machines.
Observations of multiple personality disorder as evidence of multiple software stacks on one brain.
contradictory_evidence: No direct evidence provided for AI consciousness or the existence of unthinkable thoughts.
The claim that language is a parasite is speculative and not empirically supported.

embeddable_texts: We're here at the MIT Media Lab. I'm here with Professor William Hahn. The links to his work are on screen and in the description, as well as the previous time that we spoke, which was a fantastic podcast, and I think people should check it out. Thank you so much. It's really great to speak with you again. I've been looking forward to this for some time now. Thank you. We spoke off-air yesterday and the day before. You were actually there for the Jacob Barndes podcast, which is also on screen. You had some ideas as to how to unify liveness with Stephen Wolfram's work. Please talk about that. Yeah, so really the idea is bringing together ideas from consciousness and computation. And so typically when we think of consciousness, we have this kind of light switch view that it's either on or off. And there's an idea attributed to liveness where it's really a hierarchy. It's kind of a ladder of different capabilities. And it revolves around the ability to represent your ideas, to think about your thinking, and then to think about that thinking, and so on. It's this hierarchy that goes up. And if we think about the simplest animals, they have the first order, things like sensation and response to stimulus, but they don't really have any way of representing that response. And it seems that by thinking in terms of representation, and then representing your representation, where we can have things like language, and then we can build, you know, philosophies on top of that language. And it's a way of modeling the model, and a way of talking about the talking and things. And so we get this more analog, or at least a stepwise approach to consciousness, where it's not just on or off, but it's kind of this discontinuum. And I think this is relevant now, because we're in this age where we're building intelligent machines. And I would argue that these machines that we have in the form of these modern AIs are quite intelligent. And the question now is, do they instantiate something like consciousness? And if so, is it like human consciousness? Is it something more like a lower animal, where it's just knee jerk reaction, you put in the prompt, and it just spits out the tokens? Or does it have some way of knowing what it knows and thinking about what it's thinking about? And maybe the current versions that we see right now in early 2025 don't. But it seems to me almost inevitable that if we keep going in this direction, that we will kind of close the loop on this thing. That the snake is going to bite its tail, and we will bootstrap this thing we call consciousness inside these machines. But we might need a kind of graded scale to try to understand that. And then hopefully this will help us understand things like animal consciousness, or even higher levels that human consciousness might achieve.

So when someone says that consciousness is a continuum, and it's not a binary on or off, I think you can always translate a continuum to an on or off by saying, is it zero or non-zero? So for instance, we say that a photon is chargeless. We don't say it has a little charge. Or the electron, we say it's a charged particle, even though its charge is minuscule. Right. So when you say that consciousness is a continuum and it's representations of representations, do you believe there are entities, or things, or objects, or what have you, that are not conscious? Or is it just all conscious? Well, I think that's a great question. I think that's at the heart of it, is trying to figure out does this have sort of that threshold? Do we want to think about things like rocks, for example, as being conscious? And classically, that would have been the pinnacle example of, no, clearly it's not. But I would argue that things like a modern GPU are rock-like objects, right? They're these semiconductor layers, very delicate, intricate patterns, but essentially what the classical world would say is a fancy crystal of some kind. And now we're instantiating this intelligent, possibly ultimately conscious behavior out of this rock-like object. So the situation's getting more interesting than it was previously. How does this tie into Wolfram? So Wolfram has this fantastic idea of computational equivalence. The idea is that the natural world stumbles upon computers quite often. That the idea of a universal machine that Turing established, which is a machine that can simulate any other machine. It's a machine that runs software. And in that software programming, you can get this universal machine to simulate the behavior of any other machine. And in the early days of computing, it seems like computers were very delicate human artifacts that took a lot of engineering work to put together. But what Wolfram showed with his cellular automata research is that it's relatively easy to stumble upon a system that's complex enough to support universal computation. That he has this breakdown of sort of four different classes of, he uses automata as the case study, but he argues that any system that's not obviously simple, any system that's sort of interesting in its dynamics, the majority of the time that's going to support universal computation. So in other words, that there's these natural computers all throughout nature, and previously we didn't recognize them or understand them as computational objects. I think that's what's so interesting about this new era of maybe what we might call philosophy, is that we have this new language. We can invoke the metaphor of a computer and software and program and universality where, as we spoke last time, the best minds on the planet didn't have access to those thinking tools. And so if that's really true that there's these computer-like objects all over the place, and now we have computer-like objects that might be instantiating consciousness, namely a GPU running a large language model, which obviously would be highly debated whether or not that's conscious or not. But if we take that in the abstract sense and extrapolate that out a decade or so, to me it's... it's clear that we will have a hard time, or it might be fruitless to argue whether they are or not, because they'll be so similar to the kinds of things that we see in humans that maybe they're actually all throughout nature. Maybe throughout the universe we should expect to find objects that are universal machines, sort of spontaneous in nature. And we want to think about now what's the chance, essentially, that they have a software program that might be somewhere on this ladder of consciousness that is attributed to Leibniz.

Are you referring to computational equivalence? Exactly, yeah. Okay, so in the Leibniz case you were referencing representations of representations and you have a hierarchy. Right. In the Wilfram case it sounds like you have what is not a computer, and then what exhibits computer-like qualities, and then you hit universal computer. Right. But there's nothing above that. Exactly, and that's kind of the point, is that you smash into this sort of upper ceiling of computation relatively quickly, right? It's sort of a low speed limit, and whatever vehicle you're in quickly hits that speed limit. Right, right. That's what's so profound about universality, is that's the ceiling. There's nothing more powerful than that. And so if that is relatively easy to create spontaneously, in some sense, by chance we get a computer-like object, a universal machine, then we want to think about what's the analogous part is the software that would go with it. Right? So Wilfram suggests that it's relatively easy to find computers in the wild. Well what's the chance they have any interesting programming to go with that? So is there a similar ceiling with representations? Like is it the case that once you hit the fourth representation you've hit them all, and is there a universal representation at level six? So I think you hit the nail on the head with that one, because that's really kind of what I've been thinking about. I like how you phrase it. Are humans already at that universality? Are our intellectual sphere, our language, our culture, have we maxed out? Or are we going to transcend this era, reach another level of consciousness, maybe called spirituality, whatever that might be, another layer of evolution. Or is this it? Right? That we have the ability to represent our representations and we can think about our thinking and then we can think about that and so on. And I don't know. Right? I would like to hope that we're not at that universal level yet. I think we mentioned last time on the channel this sort of path from ape to angel, right? Or from rocks to light, you know, kind of thing. Where are we on that sort of evolutionary trend in a sense? And I think that we're not at the angel stage, right? We're not quite there yet. And so it reminds me of a quote, I think they said, I forget who says it, we'll have to look it up, but we're angels with assholes. Right? That we're still these corporeal beings that eat sandwiches and have to go through our daily lives. We're not this ephemeral being that's just pure thought and energy and things. But it seems like the AI is on that trajectory. And I wonder if maybe there's just a discontinuity and as others have suggested, maybe the biological sphere just bootstraps the AI and then that's the next stage of evolution. Because for lack of a better term, they don't have assholes.

Is the question of have we hit the upper limit equivalent to the question of are there thoughts that we can't think of? So now what I mean by equivalent to is we can imagine that let's look at this room and there are thoughts everywhere and we have access to them. Okay, cool. Then there are thoughts that are outside this room. We don't have access to them. And then we'd say, okay, we have not hit the upper ceiling. And then we can say that, okay, so in that case it was, if there exists a thought that's outside this room, then we have not hit the upper ceiling. We can also say, if we have not hit the upper ceiling, it implies there is a thought that's outside this room. So I'm not sure if that's the case because then you would make an equivalence between those two. Right. Well, I do think it's the case there's unthinkable thoughts. And the question is are we able to think about them in the abstract sense? Maybe not the actual thought, but do we really understand or can we even appreciate that there's things outside of our conceptual and perceptual window? And that's what I've been thinking about a lot recently or trying to. And, you know, we mentioned last time Richard Hamming. And he talks about this idea. He says there's smells that dogs can smell that we can't smell. And they can hear things we can't hear. And there's lots of things in the animal kingdom that have a larger perceptual window. And he argues why should we think that there's thoughts we can't think? Right. It seems quite clear. And also even just arithmetically, there are numbers that we can never conceive of. At least we can write them down like Graham's number. But we can say Graham's number to the power of Graham's number. We can't actually conceive of it. We actually don't understand what it means for a number to be greater than 150 or so. Right. We can't fit these things into our mind. We can kind of only approximate them. So to someone listening, they're like, well, what are you talking about? It's quite clear. The philosophical term, I believe, is umwelt. It's quite clear our umwelt is bounded and has some overlap with other animals. I mean, that's not quite clear, but it's not obvious. Okay. So then they're thinking, okay, so what's so profound about this? Well, so thinking about these sort of unthinkable thoughts has led me in a few interesting directions. You know, why can we not get to that space? Right. I think I mentioned last time the future is not what we think it is. Because if we knew exactly which direction to go, we could just go in that direction. And so there's some kind of barrier. And the question is, is this like a natural barrier? You know, we just don't have enough neurons. We don't have enough cortical layers to represent the representations and so on. And then there could just be another hierarchy. Or something I've been thinking about more recently is that there's a more practical reason why we can't think these thoughts. And it's kind of an immune system that we mentioned before. That our mind itself is trying to protect us from a variety of thought patterns that would essentially destabilize. Both our mental patterns and then ultimately our physical self, if the thoughts go into a terrible spiral. So from an evolutionary point of view, there might be this kind of filter, this barrier that evolution has instantiated to prevent us from going nutty. And that if, from a Darwinian evolution perspective, if we just want to kind of populate the planet the best we can, you don't need this kind of intelligence. Intelligence could be kind of a Fermi-style filter that's actually preventing a lot of progress. If we think about the rain the dinosaurs had on the planet, it was 100 million years, 200 million years, and humans haven't had that kind of longevity on the planet yet. And it's hard to imagine us continuing the way we're doing for that much time. But you imagine whales and dolphins, you could easily imagine them doing the same thing they're doing for millions of years into the future and being happy to do it. But this also leads me to think about what thoughts our language supports. And I used to think that English was good enough. But now I'm not so sure. And I think what's really interesting is we've taught these language models, not just English, but all of the human languages that we could get our hands on. And I think something that's particularly relevant is the computer languages and the mathematical languages that we've also put into that system. So it has representations that it can map into English, but its mind, so to speak, doesn't really operate in English. It operates in these thought vectors, these word vectors that are independent of any particular language.

Okay, this is extremely interesting. So I have two thoughts, and you can take both of them if you like, or choose a direction. So when you said that you thought English was enough, are you saying that you thought there was something like the universal language and English is one of them, Chinese may be another. There may be some languages where they only have 100 words, and maybe those are insufficient to represent. So in other words, some people say there are some words in some languages which you cannot translate, untranslatable words. And technically, they should say they're untranslatable into another single word. And let's pick one untranslatable word. So in Turkish, there's some word for the feeling that you have after you drink coffee with friends, something like that. Let's say that. I just described it there with a set of 10 words or so. And if it was German, you would just smush them all together and make one new word out of it. Right, right. Which I think Turkish does actually as well. Okay, so is that what you meant when you were saying you thought English was enough? Right. That it was this, like you mentioned, universal software framework. That we have this idea of universal machine, but, you know, this idea of a Turing tar pit that just because everything's possible doesn't mean anything's practical with, say, like a Turing machine or some other abstract computer. And so the idea is what computer languages would be sufficient, right? So we could, as an analogy, we could say basic is not sufficiently powerful enough of a computer language to instantiate the internet or something like that. Or it might be, but it would require orders of magnitude more complexity in the coding. Whereas something like C ended up being sufficient to kind of create the modern software stack. And so I suspect now that English is not quite as universal as I previously thought it was. This is why I've been looking at things like musical languages and conlangs and esoteric languages to get some ideas about where could we put these unthinkable thoughts. Because when you learn those new languages, you can suddenly think in new, maybe more compact ways. You don't have to have a whole sentence. You can have just sort of one neuron. But like you said, I would argue that there are no untranslatable words. And if there were, you couldn't talk about them. Like at all. You wouldn't even be able to mention that they were untranslatable in some sense. And so that would be in the space of sort of maybe not unthinkable thoughts, but uncommunicatable thoughts. And one of the ideas I've been thinking about this year is the set of ideas for which you can take it apart. Like Legos, right? They have the Lego lab upstairs. And Legos you can take apart into little bricks. And like language, I have an idea in my head now. And I'm decomposing it into a serial sequence of symbols. And then you're taking those and you're putting them back together. And I hope that you get the same kind of mental representation. But you could define a set of ideas for which precisely you cannot do that, right? Where if you take any one piece, it's not the same thing anymore. That it doesn't go down into a sequence of things. And that might be, you know, it reminds me of things like gnosis, right? Knowing from the inside. Where you can't explain, you know, things like faith and God and all that. And I think a lot in the modern world, people are like, well, explain it to me. You know, explain what you mean by faith and God. And it's like, well, that's not how it works. It's precisely the kind of idea that I can't decompose into a sequence and you can put it back together. And we try. And we have religious texts and, you know, services and things that approximate it. But really the ultimate experience is of that kind where you can't do that.

Let me have fun with this immune analogy. Yeah. Is it the case then that there would be autoimmune disorders of the mind? The mind sees something that's actually benign or even salubrious or nourishing. And thinks that it's not. And so it tries to remove it. And perhaps it attacks itself in the process. It's a fantastic idea. I'd have to think about that a little more. But I think in some sense, absolutely. That there's going to be. And that might be kind of the basis for mental diversity and mental disorders. If we might call them that. Because now we're better understanding language than ever before. By building these machines that instantiate language. It gives us this petri dish, this microscope. And I think when there's a lot of mystery around how these language models operate. And I think the real mystery is in the words, in the language. We didn't understand what words were. We didn't really understand what language was. And we thought it was this communication kind of thing. And I've been thinking about it more with my colleague, Dr. Behrenholz. As an organism. Something that's alive. And that we need to invoke the framework from biology to think about it. Not just as communication. But as a, I've referred to it as a parasite in some sense. And not necessarily pejorative. I've referred to it as a divine parasite. But it's something that lives on the brain. But it's not the brain. And one of the ways I've been thinking about this is with things like multiple personality syndrome and split personality syndrome. That I think those are evidence that when I'm talking to you now, I'm not talking to your brain. I'm talking to this entity that lives in your brain. And when we see people with multiple personalities, it's clear that they're instantiating more than one operating system, software, stack. On the same hardware. And they're multiplexed. Like we run more than one app on our phone at a time. That the brain is rich enough of a substrate, of a backdrop, to have multiple plays unfolding at the same time. And then this leads into kind of the other side of unthinkable thoughts and this immune system concept. In areas of things like mind control. And is our brain a programmable object? And if so, is language, is natural language, a programming language?

chunks.text: We're here at the MIT Media Lab. I'm here with Professor William Hahn. The links to his work are on screen and in the description, as well as the previous time that we spoke, which was a fantastic podcast, and I think people should check it out. Thank you so much. It's really great to speak with you again. I've been looking forward to this for some time now. Thank you. We spoke off-air yesterday and the day before. It's really great to speak with you again. I've been looking forward to this for some time now. Thank you. We spoke off-air yesterday and the day before. You were actually there for the Jacob Barndes podcast, which is also on screen. You had some ideas as to how to unify liveness with Stephen Wolfram's work. Please talk about that. Yeah, so really the idea is bringing together ideas from consciousness and computation. And so typically when we think of consciousness, we have this kind of light switch view that it's either on or off. And there's an idea attributed to liveness where it's really a hierarchy. It's kind of a ladder of different capabilities. And it revolves around the ability to represent your ideas, to think about your thinking, and then to think about that thinking, and so on. It's this hierarchy that goes up. And if we think about the simplest animals, they have the first order, things like sensation and response to stimulus, but they don't really have any way of representing that response. And it seems that by thinking in terms of representation, and then representing your representation, where we can have things like language, and then we can build, you know, philosophies on top of that language. And it's a way of modeling the model, and a way of talking about the talking and things. And so we get this more analog, or at least a stepwise approach to consciousness, where it's not just on or off, but it's kind of this discontinuum. And I think this is relevant now, because we're in this age where we're building intelligent machines. classification.rationale: Public-facing interview or panel transcript featuring Jacques Vallee, Robert Bigelow, and Colm Kelleher discussing NIDS, Skinwalker Ranch, AAWSAP, disclosure, consciousness, and alleged anomalous effects. It contains historical recollections and extraordinary claims rather than a primary government or scientific record. Transcript errors, phonetic misspellings, and absent source metadata warrant cautious ingestion.

source_provenance.transcript_status: Supplied transcript is truncated and appears machine-generated or lightly edited

basis: The speakers make first-person claims about their own employment, organizational roles, and participation in NIDS and the program transcribed as OSAP.
Named people, organizations, dates, and claimed document counts provide externally traceable details.
The excerpt supplies no original contracts, government records, technical reports, sensor data, medical records, or chain-of-custody documentation.
Claims involving extraterrestrial consciousness, telepathy, psychokinesis, paranormal effects, and anomalous camera behavior are presented without test data in this excerpt.
The host sometimes frames historical influence more strongly than the guests; Robert Bigelow qualifies the host's causal account by saying NIDS only 'helped' and was not exclusively responsible.

issues: The transcript contains probable transcription errors in personal names and acronyms, including 'Colum Keller,' 'Bigalow,' 'Valet,' 'Heinik,' 'OSAP,' 'OAP,' and 'Gary Noland.'
Likely intended forms require verification against the video and authoritative records.
Speaker labels are absent, making attribution dependent on conversational context.
The source ends with a pipeline truncation marker and an incomplete sentence.
No classification markings, redactions, document headers, or page identifiers are visible in the supplied text.

claimed_sensitive_material: A majority of the program's claimed technical work product is said not to have been publicly released.
A joking exchange refers to top-secret clearances for a fictitious moonshine program; context indicates humor rather than a substantive classified-program claim.
classification_assessment.note: No inference about classification status can be made from non-release alone.

notes: The interview revisits established NIDS, Skinwalker Ranch, AAWSAP/AATIP, New York Times, Tic Tac, and disclosure narratives.

Potentially new material includes the described trust and foundation structure, projected liquidity, Vallée's claimed return to a French space-agency committee, and Bigelow's claimed meeting with the president.
The excerpt does not establish whether these details appeared previously in other interviews or publications.

methodological_assessment.government: The discussion names a DIA-associated program and unreleased technical products but provides no award documents, task orders, classification guides, official correspondence, or release records.
methodological_assessment.witness: Kelleher gives a detailed career chronology and estimates approximately 300 days and nights at Skinwalker Ranch, but observation conditions and individual incidents are not described. Vallée discusses witness trauma generally without presenting case files or clinical assessments.
methodological_assessment.scientific: No experimental protocol, control design, statistical analysis, peer-review status, calibration record, or reproducible dataset is supplied. Proposed links among consciousness, a unified field theory, telepathy, and UFO effects remain assertions or hypotheses in this excerpt.
methodological_assessment.media: The format is a friendly panel interview among long-standing associates. The host uses disclosure-oriented framing and offers causal interpretations that are not independently established within the excerpt.
methodological_assessment.historical: The speakers provide a chronology linking NIDS, Skinwalker Ranch, a DIA-associated program, Bigelow Aerospace, and later consciousness research. It has lead value but does not itself authenticate the institutional history.
methodological_assessment.technical: References to cameras, power depletion, life-support systems, physiological effects, and objects outperforming fighter jets lack metadata, specifications, telemetry, environmental controls, or instrument-failure analysis.

supporting_evidence.claim_supported: Kelleher participated in NIDS and later managed day-to-day operations of the program transcribed as OSAP.
supporting_evidence.source_derived_support: Kelleher gives a first-person chronology beginning in August 1996, describes work at Skinwalker Ranch, and states that he later reported to Robert Bigelow while running program operations.

supporting_evidence.claim_supported: NIDS experience influenced the later government-associated program.
supporting_evidence.source_derived_support: Kelleher explicitly states that physiological, psychological, and alleged paranormal effects studied through NIDS informed the later program's approach.

supporting_evidence.claim_supported: The program generated a substantial technical-document collection.
supporting_evidence.source_derived_support: Kelleher estimates approximately 100 technical documents and says roughly 35 to 38 were released.

supporting_evidence.claim_supported: Vallée had a role in the NIDS science advisory board.
supporting_evidence.source_derived_support: The participants discuss a group photograph of the advisory board, and Kelleher addresses Vallée as a regular influence at board meetings.

contradictory_evidence.target_claim: The current disclosure process and associated developments began directly and primarily with NIDS.
contradictory_evidence.source_derived_counterpoint: After the host attributes later developments to the NIDS group, Bigelow responds that they 'definitely helped' but says their role was not exclusive and credits other researchers.

contradictory_evidence.target_claim: The phenomenon is now established in a scientifically decisive sense.
contradictory_evidence.source_derived_counterpoint: Vallée says authorities and parts of academia recognize the subject as real, while also saying the phenomenon must still be reassessed and requires new tools. No decisive dataset is presented in the excerpt.

contradictory_evidence.target_claim: Observed effects necessarily demonstrate non-human technology or intelligence.
contradictory_evidence.source_derived_counterpoint: Kelleher says he saw things he could not explain, which establishes reported uncertainty rather than an identified cause.

inference_notes: Inference: The interview has useful entity, chronology, and document-discovery value but low evidentiary value for extraordinary physical or biological claims.
Inference: The acronym rendered as 'OSAP' is likely a transcription error, possibly referring to AAWSAP, but this must be checked against the audio and official documents.

Inference: Claims that cameras or batteries can be intentionally manipulated should first be tested against ordinary equipment failure, battery condition, temperature, electromagnetic interference, operator error, and selection bias.
Inference: References to trauma or physiological effects do not identify a cause. Medical, environmental, psychological, and conventional exposure explanations require case-level review.
Inference: Recognition of UAP as a legitimate subject of inquiry does not establish extraterrestrial origin, telepathy, or non-human intelligence.
Inference: The interview's congenial format and shared institutional history may reduce adversarial questioning and increase the need for independent corroboration.
follow_up_needed: Obtain the complete video, verify speaker identities and the transcript against the audio, and capture the channel name, publication date, description, and any linked primary documents before ingestion.
Verify Kelleher's employment and roles through NIDS records, the relevant DIA contract and task documentation, Bigelow Aerospace records, and contemporaneous biographies.
Resolve all acronyms and names, especially whether 'OSAP' means AAWSAP and whether references to AATIP are being used distinctly or interchangeably.
Create a document-level inventory of the claimed approximately 100 technical products and reconcile it with the claimed 35 to 38 public releases.
Verify Vallée's claimed reappointment to the relevant French space-agency committee through CNES or GEIPAN records.
Verify the legal existence, directors, mission statements, tax status, and funding claims of Bigelow's trust and two 501(c)(3) foundations.
Seek independent documentation of Bigelow's claimed presidential meeting and identify which president, meeting date, attendees, and materials were provided.
For any physiological or psychological-effect claims, require de-identified case records, diagnostic criteria, exposure timelines, comparison groups, and alternative-cause assessments.
For any sensor or performance claims, obtain original files, metadata, calibration histories, platform data, environmental conditions, and chain-of-custody records.
Run duplicate detection against earlier NIDS, Skinwalker Ranch, AAWSAP/AATIP, and Bigelow interviews to isolate genuinely new statements.

Maybe it's my you know training in in astronomy but in the universe there is nothing abnormal. Everything is normal. We just don't recognize it. You know we we didn't know that there were galaxies outside our own. We didn't know about, you know, dark matter. We didn't know about all those things. And they are not abnormal. classification.rationale: Public-facing interview or panel transcript featuring Jacques Vallee, Robert Bigelow, and Colm Kelleher discussing NIDS, Skinwalker Ranch, AAWSAP, disclosure, consciousness, and alleged anomalous effects. It contains historical recollections and extraordinary claims rather than a primary government or scientific record. Transcript errors, phonetic misspellings, and absent source metadata warrant cautious ingestion.

source_provenance.transcript_status: Supplied transcript is truncated and appears machine-generated or lightly edited

basis: The speakers make first-person claims about their own employment, organizational roles, and participation in NIDS and the program transcribed as OSAP.
Named people, organizations, dates, and claimed document counts provide externally traceable details.
The excerpt supplies no original contracts, government records, technical reports, sensor data, medical records, or chain-of-custody documentation.
Claims involving extraterrestrial consciousness, telepathy, psychokinesis, paranormal effects, and anomalous camera behavior are presented without test data in this excerpt.
The host sometimes frames historical influence more strongly than the guests; Robert Bigelow qualifies the host's causal account by saying NIDS only 'helped' and was not exclusively responsible.

issues: The transcript contains probable transcription errors in personal names and acronyms, including 'Colum Keller,' 'Bigalow,' 'Valet,' 'Heinik,' 'OSAP,' 'OAP,' and 'Gary Noland.'
Likely intended forms require verification against the video and authoritative records.
Speaker labels are absent, making attribution dependent on conversational context.
The source ends with a pipeline truncation marker and an incomplete sentence.
No classification markings, redactions, document headers, or page identifiers are visible in the supplied text.

claimed_sensitive_material: A majority of the program's claimed technical work product is said not to have been publicly released.
A joking exchange refers to top-secret clearances for a fictitious moonshine program; context indicates humor rather than a substantive classified-program claim.
classification_assessment.note: No inference about classification status can be made from non-release alone.

notes: The interview revisits established NIDS, Skinwalker Ranch, AAWSAP/AATIP, New York Times, Tic Tac, and disclosure narratives.

Potentially new material includes the described trust and foundation structure, projected liquidity, Vallée's claimed return to a French space-agency committee, and Bigelow's claimed meeting with the president.
The excerpt does not establish whether these details appeared previously in other interviews or publications.

methodological_assessment.government: The discussion names a DIA-associated program and unreleased technical products but provides no award documents, task orders, classification guides, official correspondence, or release records.
methodological_assessment.witness: Kelleher gives a detailed career chronology and estimates approximately 300 days and nights at Skinwalker Ranch, but observation conditions and individual incidents are not described. Vallée discusses witness trauma generally without presenting case files or clinical assessments.
methodological_assessment.scientific: No experimental protocol, control design, statistical analysis, peer-review status, calibration record, or reproducible dataset is supplied. Proposed links among consciousness, a unified field theory, telepathy, and UFO effects remain assertions or hypotheses in this excerpt.
methodological_assessment.media: The format is a friendly panel interview among long-standing associates. The host uses disclosure-oriented framing and offers causal interpretations that are not independently established within the excerpt.
methodological_assessment.historical: The speakers provide a chronology linking NIDS, Skinwalker Ranch, a DIA-associated program, Bigelow Aerospace, and later consciousness research. It has lead value but does not itself authenticate the institutional history.
methodological_assessment.technical: References to cameras, power depletion, life-support systems, physiological effects, and objects outperforming fighter jets lack metadata, specifications, telemetry, environmental controls, or instrument-failure analysis.

supporting_evidence.claim_supported: Kelleher participated in NIDS and later managed day-to-day operations of the program transcribed as OSAP.
supporting_evidence.source_derived_support: Kelleher gives a first-person chronology beginning in August 1996, describes work at Skinwalker Ranch, and states that he later reported to Robert Bigelow while running program operations.

supporting_evidence.claim_supported: NIDS experience influenced the later government-associated program.
supporting_evidence.source_derived_support: Kelleher explicitly states that physiological, psychological, and alleged paranormal effects studied through NIDS informed the later program's approach.

supporting_evidence.claim_supported: The program generated a substantial technical-document collection.
supporting_evidence.source_derived_support: Kelleher estimates approximately 100 technical documents and says roughly 35 to 38 were released.

supporting_evidence.claim_supported: Vallée had a role in the NIDS science advisory board.
supporting_evidence.source_derived_support: The participants discuss a group photograph of the advisory board, and Kelleher addresses Vallée as a regular influence at board meetings.

contradictory_evidence.target_claim: The current disclosure process and associated developments began directly and primarily with NIDS.
contradictory_evidence.source_derived_counterpoint: After the host attributes later developments to the NIDS group, Bigelow responds that they 'definitely helped' but says their role was not exclusive and credits other researchers.

contradictory_evidence.target_claim: The phenomenon is now established in a scientifically decisive sense.
contradictory_evidence.source_derived_counterpoint: Vallée says authorities and parts of academia recognize the subject as real, while also saying the phenomenon must still be reassessed and requires new tools. No decisive dataset is presented in the excerpt.

contradictory_evidence.target_claim: Observed effects necessarily demonstrate non-human technology or intelligence.
contradictory_evidence.source_derived_counterpoint: Kelleher says he saw things he could not explain, which establishes reported uncertainty rather than an identified cause.

inference_notes: Inference: The interview has useful entity, chronology, and document-discovery value but low evidentiary value for extraordinary physical or biological claims.
Inference: The acronym rendered as 'OSAP' is likely a transcription error, possibly referring to AAWSAP, but this must be checked against the audio and official documents.

Inference: Claims that cameras or batteries can be intentionally manipulated should first be tested against ordinary equipment failure, battery condition, temperature, electromagnetic interference, operator error, and selection bias.
Inference: References to trauma or physiological effects do not identify a cause. Medical, environmental, psychological, and conventional exposure explanations require case-level review.
Inference: Recognition of UAP as a legitimate subject of inquiry does not establish extraterrestrial origin, telepathy, or non-human intelligence.
Inference: The interview's congenial format and shared institutional history may reduce adversarial questioning and increase the need for independent corroboration.
follow_up_needed: Obtain the complete video, verify speaker identities and the transcript against the audio, and capture the channel name, publication date, description, and any linked primary documents before ingestion.
Verify Kelleher's employment and roles through NIDS records, the relevant DIA contract and task documentation, Bigelow Aerospace records, and contemporaneous biographies.
Resolve all acronyms and names, especially whether 'OSAP' means AAWSAP and whether references to AATIP are being used distinctly or interchangeably.
Create a document-level inventory of the claimed approximately 100 technical products and reconcile it with the claimed 35 to 38 public releases.
Verify Vallée's claimed reappointment to the relevant French space-agency committee through CNES or GEIPAN records.
Verify the legal existence, directors, mission statements, tax status, and funding claims of Bigelow's trust and two 501(c)(3) foundations.
Seek independent documentation of Bigelow's claimed presidential meeting and identify which president, meeting date, attendees, and materials were provided.
For any physiological or psychological-effect claims, require de-identified case records, diagnostic criteria, exposure timelines, comparison groups, and alternative-cause assessments.
For any sensor or performance claims, obtain original files, metadata, calibration histories, platform data, environmental conditions, and chain-of-custody records.
Run duplicate detection against earlier NIDS, Skinwalker Ranch, AAWSAP/AATIP, and Bigelow interviews to isolate genuinely new statements.

chunks.text: Robert, we've got a full house here today. You know, I think people, some people describe the current time as the age of disclosure. It certainly is an age of transition. And we're going to hear from today. You're joined by two of our closest friends and most trusted colleagues and and the smartest guys we know. you can introduce your your colleague here first and then we'll meet our special guest. >> Well, this is Dr. Colum Keller. Um he is going to expand on all of his activities over the years as different categories of what he's been involved in. But um one of the mo very important ones is that uh 2 or 3 years ago I put together a revocable trust uh which upon my passing becomes irrevocable and then I uh formed uh two 501c3 foundations. One is a medical foundation and it's fairly parochial as to what you would expect. The educational foundation is the other one and that is not a normal educational uh traditional kind of format. So the educational foundation's focus exclusively is on the survival of human consciousness uh and what consciousness is all about in that context and it also involves the consciousness of other uh intelligent beings uh such as ETSs in particular not whales or dolphins or anything like that but ET consciousness as well as human consciousness the survival of it and so that is the exclusive mission of the educational foundation. The importance of this is that potentially uh the educational foundation will have over a billion dollars liquidity uh to use uh hopefully responsibly uh in furthering the um the understanding of human survival and the understanding of of consciousness and the understanding of consciousness on the other side as it pertains to the universe. and perhaps uh leading to a supreme conscious consciousness as we said in an earlier um broadcast a god force is not that word is not sufficient as to the power behind what we're talking about. So in the theory of everything that solution probably is all this time that's been latent in in exposing this disc discussion is consciousness in the equation and then I think you would have the theory of everything you would have a unified field theory if that were incorporated into intentionality and the creativity aspects of things and that's what consciousness can do. So having said all that, Colum is um a director. We have three directors of the of the trust and of each of the foundations. And Colum sits on the board of all three. >> You didn't give him the keys to the bank accounts. >> Never. No, not even close. Oh my gosh. No. That's got iron steel bars on >> waiting for the election. >> That's right. That's right. Um so he's Colum is a very valuable individual all the way around. and he's he's a really good thinker and he's uh uh and he'll explain his background. So, I'm going to shut up and let him talk.

chunks.heading_path: Colum Keller biography, NIDS, Skinwalker Ranch, and OSAP
chunks.text: >> Well, thanks for that very very nice introduction. Um I was just thinking that it's been exactly 30 years to the month >> since I first joined the National Institute for Discovery Science. It was August of 1996. Goes back a long way. But I was working as a mainstream immunologist in in the National Jewish Center in Denver, [clears throat] background in biochemistry, immunology, molecular biology, when I I caught sight of a a really unusual ad in Science magazine, and the the ad said, "We're looking for scientists to explore the evolution and um origin of consciousness in the universe. So, this is a in the middle of ads for molecular biology technicians and this kind of thing. So, I just couldn't resist it. I picked up the phone and um eventually I got talking to Robert Bigalow, flew out to Las Vegas and um within a very short period of time I was hired in August of 1996 and um Robert had just purchased the uh 500 acre property in northeastern Utah which became globally renowned as Skinwalker Ranch. And so within a few weeks I and two other scientists were on Skinwalker Ranch. We I think over the six years I spent about 300 days and nights on Skinwalker Ranch. Saw a lot of stuff that I was not you know I was not able to explain. And then later I think you guys have already discussed the OSAP program with DIA. I was um running the day-to-day operations uh reporting to Robert Bigalow of the OSAP program. We had 50 um scientists and technicians and counter intelligence people, security people um investigating UFOs. It was the largest I think UFO program that has been admitted to in the history of the UFO phenomenon with respect to the United States government. So we spent two and two and a half years just under two and a half years doing that. Um we produced about a hundred separate technical documents that um very few of which have ever been released about I think 35 to 38 of those have been released but the majority of of our work product has never been released. And then um after that I was uh managing the uh life support systems group at Bigalow Aerospace in charge of basically 11 different systems that cumulatively astronauts use to keep alive in low earth orbit. And then um since then I've been with the Bigalow Institute for um consciousness studies. So, it's been a long very career uh with Robert Bigalow and it's been 30 years of extraordinary fun. >> Was the still as far as the life support systems, the still that produced the excellent whiskey? Was that also essential? >> That was the uh that was the sort of the hidden program we were we had to have top secret security clearances >> in order to generate [clears throat] the uh moonshine. >> Hardly anybody knew about that. >> That's right. It's the only way of keeping astronauts, you know. >> That's right. >> Attention and alive. >> Yeah.

chunks.text: >> We're also joined today by someone else who was there at the beginning of NIDS 30 years ago this year. January of 1996. The science advisory board had its first meeting here. And I knew the names that were I walked into this room, I knew a lot of the names, but there was only one of the faces I knew and it was Dr. Jacques Valet. And I was he he uh I I am an unabashed fan, Jacques. Um, I've I have an entire shelf of your books. I think you're you're the best writer and deepest thinker in the whole topic of eupfology, but it's your life has been so much more than that. You know, you what what' you hand them? >> This is a photograph of most of the group at one time that we took of the science advisory board of NIDS. Jank is in here >> along along with with well there are three or four people that happen to be missing out of here. Uh some of them one or two intentionally because they didn't want to be photographed. [laughter] >> Well, I think we know who they are. >> Yeah. Well, it's a it's a day of transition, a time of transition for you. Age of disclosure, but an age of of transition for you. You're making some moves. Uh, Forbidden Science is the latest volume of your journals to come out and it's an extraordinary account of of your travels, your interactions with scientists, investigators, agencies, uh, your pursuit of cases. Uh, and it I what I like most about it is you incorporate what else is going on in the world. This is not talking about a this UFO crash or that UFO theory or something like that. and we'll dive into as much of this as we can today, but it kind of represents the uh the end of a chapter for you. This this is going to be the last one. Why did you make that decision or was it hard? >> It's not the end of my research. It's the end of my writing because I think we're at a point, you know, where certainly two important things have happened. chunks.heading_path: Interdisciplinary investigation, witness trauma, and biological complexity
chunks.text: >> You know, I think this was all coming together just at the right time, you know, and uh what what you saw was that the the the problem was not going to be solved by by the government. It was not going to be solved by people in physics or in one discipline that you really needed to assemble people from different different areas including consciousness because as you know uh when you go to investigate a sighting you find people in distress you know you don't you find I'm not talking about the military side they may be in in distress in other ways is because of the instruments, because of everything else and the danger that they are exposed to. But the farmer in the field, you know, at first he'll just say, well, it was a light and so on. If you spend enough time with with him or his family, then you find that there is a profound trauma behind what they are just describing. And this is not something that I can, you know, that I can analyze. I can analyze what psychologists or what biologists, what medical people, what consciousness researchers can tell me should go into the database at some point. And that's, you know, the road that we've traveled together. That's that's maybe the brilliance of your books and your approach to the topic is, you know, you start out as an astronomer looking at data that was being destroyed and were curious about why other astronomers wouldn't want to be studying this. I mean, as you write in another of your book, the one with Heinek, uh that's why you're a scientist is to explore mysteries, things you don't know. Um, you know, you looked at the sort of the the organic picture of it's not just sensor data, photos, videos, um, crash materials, whatever. It's how our interaction works, how it affects us over the long run. The idea of a control system, right? And that's one thing that's missing from everything you see on TV today and most of the discussion is it's always, you know, who should be looking at this and and how does it change and so on. You never talk about how we're going to be changed by what we see. You know certainly in biology I mean the the new generation of biologists has been humbled by the you know I talked to professor Gary Noland at Stanford you know we work on the the you know on on the material side of of all this but we also talk about the biological side and he is in you know amazed is in continuous amazement by what is beyond the genome. I mean the genome we haven't completely as as you know better than I do you know understood what it does >> but beyond the genome there is a proteome and there you know all these other levels and the question is you know as you said where are the hundreds of bright young scientists who need to come into the field to open up all these new disciplines. It's not just a new experiment. It's a new field, you know, at every level. And u we certainly 10 years ago, we didn't have the the tools to even describe what that was. And uh now we're beginning to have the tools to >> to engage it. And we need to do the same thing with UFOs. We're very late. You know, we've been set back several times. And uh now we we just need to to move forward.

chunks.heading_path: NIDS legacy, consciousness, and paranormal research
chunks.text: >> I don't I know Robert you don't like to pat yourself on the back too much but if you think back to the time when the three of you were part of NIDS starting this 30 years ago now uh the profound changes that are that can directly be linked to that work. I mean, NIDS becomes a model for Osap um with no OAP. There's no ATIP, there's no New York Times story, there's no Tic Tac case investigation, none of that stuff. And the things that are unfolding now, the changes that are underway started with you guys here in this building 30 years ago. We definitely helped. Well, we, you know, it wasn't exclusive. The the uh we [clears throat] we were benefited by some very bright bright people in our organization and uh a lot of good researchers were were there and and also we we tapped into um other kinds of paranormal activities that human beings are capable of. Uh claroyance, precognition, remote viewing, those kinds of things. Um and so we tapped into that to get a sense of what's what how can we understand what is out there that is of a of a foreign intelligence that is all telepathic. Uh I I think it's pretty much 100% telepathic. I don't know of any any kind kind of uh conversation that is otherwise. Uh so so [clears throat] then thought to try to understand um what you can do with with thought in a micro or macro PK kind of situation for example [clears throat] is is outside of our our traditional education in any university is it's not there you know so where do you go to learn these kinds of things and so it it was a lot of fun that's all I remember it as being an exciting time all the time >> and same for you column especially once you once you get to the ranch.

chunks.heading_path: Keller on NIDS experience and OSAP human-effects research
chunks.text: >> Yeah, I I think the National Institute for Discovery Science was incredibly valuable in terms of um all of the experience that we gained over time. I mean we were very much influenced by you Jacques because you were part of the science advisory board and very regular meetings and you know we we started the OSAP program with a wealth of experience that we learned from National Institute for Discovery Science and we were very much um looking at the effects of UFOs on people even as the OSAP program started and that was because of what we had learned at at NIDS and you We were looking at physiological effects of UFOs. We were looking at psychological effects and inevitably as Robert has has said uh paranormal effects. Um so we saw this as a as a continuum. It was not only a machine in the sky that was um performing all outperforming all of our fighter jets. it actually had effects on humans um which could be documented at the physiological level and even the psychological level. So um I think the NIDS experience was very valuable in starting off the OSAP program. >> I got to give other people not belonging to NIDS like Bud Hopkins and John Mack credit too because we learned a lot from those guys. you know, we sponsored uh their work in different ways and uh they were they were good researchers, really good. >> Earlier this year, Stephen Spielberg came out with his long anticipated uh uh movie Disclosure Day. Just the title alone got the UFO world kind of pretty excited. I was hoping to see the the character of Lome revisit that film and and show up. What' you think of the film and was it appropriate for the time given that disclosures on it's it's page one news again it the public is engaged Congress is asking questions there are programs that we can get into and talk about. Um but you had mentioned when we started the conversation that the page has turned. Is there no stuffing the genie back in the bottle from here on out? And what would disclosure look like to you? What what needs to be disclosed to count as disclosure?

chunks.heading_path: Disclosure, normality, and reassessing the phenomenon
chunks.text: What's what's the most interesting thing to me um in in the new Spielberg movie is that there are no UFOs. I mean there is a shape of something at the end but it's irrelevant because now we we know they exist and the problem is how do we deal with that you know on the human level with all the parasychology things that all the psychic effects that happen that we didn't anticipate and and with all the politics and all the intricate games that people are going to about it. So it's it's a very different movie, you know. Um I think now the the the the problem is one of reassessing what the um you know what the phenomenon consists of uh on on our terms. And the the one place where I would bounce the ball with you is when we use the word abnormal or paranormal in in the universe. Maybe it's my you know training in in astronomy but in the universe there is nothing abnormal. Everything is normal. We just don't recognize it. You know we we didn't know that there were galaxies outside our own. We didn't know about, you know, dark matter. We didn't know about all those things. And they are not abnormal. They were there before. Uh they were there billions of years before. Uh we just were not aware of them. And that's going to be the same the same thing with this, you know, as we get into it. So we we need yes we we need to bring in well-trained people with an open mind but you know the experience that you know we had with the the 50 60 people that the two of you recruited okay to work at bus it took them two years to really understand the problem you know they went to Brazil they didn't understand what they saw in Brazil Okay. Uh they uh they they were designing instruments but those instruments were remember when we had that session about putting cameras on the ranch uh to see what would happen to the the animals if something came in. And I [clears throat] made the point that you needed another circle of cameras to watch the cameras >> because there is no such thing as a normal experiment.

I mean, I to me the the public now that's the loudest. Anything less than show me the bodies and show me the saucers, the crashes, is going to fall short. And I just can't imagine that happening. And I'd be curious from all three of you, what would happen if it did? How would the public react? What would be the effect?

Um as I we've said before, we have much more to fear from ourselves than we do from AT up to this point in time. Right? So it have to be in order for the public to to uh really I think uh come loose. It has to be something that [clears throat] is terrifying that um we have never seen before and that we would not anticipate ever happening because I don't think it's in the best interest of ETSs themselves of wasting 80 years of time in the modern era to expose themselves to do so many demonstrations to be so involved in multiple kinds of phenomenal kinds of activities uh in many in just thousands of different ways. Um it would be cons completely inconsistent with all the past behavior. It would make absolutely no sense whatsoever. So I think people underestimate the public's general capacity to accept and recognize the uniqueness of what's going on and then maybe start to have a hunger for learning more and more about it because how can there not be enormous curiosity? And this includes our science communities, you know, that the the egos of scientists is insufferable sometimes, right? So, we know that.
